rationale: The anger of the surrounding nations follows the rebuilding of the altar and its joyful dedication described in the preceding chapter.

Both accounts describe attacks on Jewish communities living among other peoples; the Joppa killings and Jamnia plot illustrate the same danger without identifying them with all the attacks summarized here.

Both accounts present Judas attacking Idumeans who were oppressing Israel; the source names Akrabattene, while the target describes assaults on fortresses and gives a casualty total. The differing campaign settings remain distinct.
Both accounts describe hostile groups sheltering in towers that Maccabeus captures with lethal force; the sons of Baean are not identified with the unnamed occupants of the two Idumean towers.

Both accounts place a substantial army under a commander named Timothy opposite Judas; this compares the campaign narratives without resolving every occurrence of Timothy into one chronological biography.
Moses's men previously captured Jazer and its dependent villages; Judas's seizure of Jazer and its daughter towns recalls conquest of the same named district in a later conflict.
The Israelites' flight into the stronghold establishes the danger that Judas later interrupts when he finds the enemy attacking its defenders.
The written appeal from endangered Jews leads to the assembly's decision to send Judas and Jonathan to Gilead and Simon to Galilee.
The letter warns of Timothy's coming assault on the stronghold; Judas later arrives during that assault and routs Timothy's army.
The petition to rescue the threatened brothers receives its narrative answer when Judas orders his men to fight for their brothers and drives the attackers away.
The messengers' report of distress in Galilee leads to Simon's campaign and evacuation of the Galilean families into Judea.
The threat from Ptolemais and the surrounding region is answered by Simon's pursuit to Ptolemais and removal of the endangered Galilean population.
The division of the rescue mission is fulfilled by Simon's Galilean campaign and Judas and Jonathan's crossing of the Jordan.
The two commanders entrusted with guarding Judea later leave that task to seek military fame, ending in the defeat attributed to their disobedience.
Judas's explicit prohibition on starting a battle explains why the later offensive and defeat of Joseph and Azariah are judged disobedient.
Simon's Galilean battles carry out the rescue assignment prompted by reports that the surrounding peoples intended to destroy the Jews there.
Simon's removal of the Galilean families and belongings to Judea parallels Judas's gathering of the Gileadite families and possessions for the same destination.
The sudden turn toward Bosora responds to the report that Jews were confined in that named city and that the strongholds faced imminent destruction.
The siege equipment and attack that Judas sees confirm the danger described in the earlier letter from those who had fled into the stronghold.
The command to fight for their brothers directly answers those brothers' appeal for rescue from the enemy's hand.
Judas's three divisions, trumpets, and shouted appeal recall Gideon's three companies sounding trumpets before the enemy's flight; the circumstances and equipment are not identical.
Both accounts portray Timothy's forces fleeing before Judas and suffering heavy losses; the reported totals differ and are not harmonized.
The scouts' report that the surrounding nations have gathered under Timothy renews the coalition threat already described by the trapped Israelites.
Timothy predicts defeat if Judas crosses first; Judas then prevents delay, crosses first, and puts the opposing nations to flight.
Timothy hopes Judas will hesitate and camp beyond the water, but Judas forbids camping and takes the initiative by crossing immediately.
Judas's order not to encamp defeats the alternative on which Timothy based his hope of victory and leads to the first crossing Timothy feared.

Both campaign accounts describe Timothy's army fleeing at Judas's advance in a setting involving a refuge named Carnaim here and Carnion there; the names and routes are preserved without asserting exact identity.
Judas's gathering of Gileadite families and possessions for Judah matches Simon's earlier evacuation of Galilean families and property into Judea.
Both accounts identify Ephron as a fortified city encountered by Judas's forces; each supplies different details about its defenses and the surrounding campaign.
Ephron's refusal of passage belongs to a sequence like Sihon's refusal of Israel's peaceful transit, which is followed in each narrative by armed conflict.
Judas's peaceful request to pass on foot echoes Moses's peaceful proposal to Sihon to pass through his land without turning aside; both requests are refused.
Both passages join envoys or peaceful words, a request to pass through another territory, and the inhabitants' refusal of transit.
Both accounts describe the capture of fortified Ephron by Judas's forces; this account specifies a day-and-night assault, while the other emphasizes prayer and gives a casualty figure.
After passage is refused, Judas takes the obstructing city and passes through it; Israel likewise defeats Sihon and takes his towns after his refusal of passage.
Both armies respond with an offering after finding that none of their men is missing; Numbers describes a gift for atonement and this account describes joyful whole burnt offerings.
Joseph and Azariah's desire to imitate the brothers' exploits is set against their original assignment to guard the people and avoid battle until Judas returns.
The commanders' wish to make a name for themselves repeats the builders' ambition at Babel; in each narrative the self-promoting project ends in failure.
The march against Jamnia directly violates Judas's earlier instruction not to engage the surrounding nations before his return.
Both accounts depict Gorgias opposing Jewish forces, but the commanders, course of combat, and setting differ; this comparison does not merge the two battles.
Joseph and Azariah's unauthorized attack ends in rout, as the Israelites' advance after Moses's warning ends in defeat; the comparison concerns disobedient initiative rather than identical battles.
Both narratives explain military defeat through disregard of the leader's warning against an unauthorized advance.

Mattathias had assigned counsel to Simon and command against the nations to Judas, providing the earlier family commission behind the distinction drawn here between the brothers and the defeated commanders.
The widespread honour of Judas and his brothers develops the earlier account of Judas extending his people's glory and becoming renowned to the ends of the earth.
Both accounts describe Judas attacking Idumean defenses in response to conflict with the Jews; this verse names Hebron and its dependent towns, which the other account does not specify.
The priests' fatal venture to perform brave deeds without counsel repeats the chapter's warning through Joseph and Azariah's self-promoting, disobedient expedition.
Judas's demolition of pagan altars and burning of carved divine images correspond closely to the law's instructions to pull down such altars and burn such images.
Both accounts place Antiochus in Persia before a failed attack on a temple-rich city; this text names Elymais and the other Persepolis, so the locations are not silently equated.
The temple weapons are attributed to Alexander son of Philip, the Macedonian first ruler of the Greeks, identifying the conqueror introduced at the book's opening.
Both accounts describe Antiochus attempting to plunder a city's temple and being resisted by its inhabitants; their city names differ.
Both describe Antiochus's humiliating retreat after local resistance, but this account points toward Babylon and the other next locates him at Ecbatana.
Both bring the king news of military reverses involving the Jews during his eastern retreat; the other account names Nicanor and Timothy, while the following verse here names Lysias.
The report that Lysias's strong army was driven back recalls his defeat near Beth-zur and withdrawal to Antioch.
The report that the profaning installation was removed recalls the cleansing of the sanctuary and dismantling of the defiled altar before its replacement.
The report of high sanctuary walls and Beth-zur's fortification recalls the defensive works built after the dedication.
Both portray Antiochus becoming gravely ill after his reverses, but this text stresses sorrow and frustrated plans while the other describes bodily affliction as divine judgment.
Both accounts present the ailing Antiochus despairing of his condition; the other account additionally introduces his letter to the Jews.
Antiochus's claim to have ruled kindly can be compared with his letter's claims of benefits, fairness, and humanity; these are the king's self-descriptions within narratives critical of his conduct.
Antiochus's recollection of taking Jerusalem's silver and gold vessels points back to the narrated plundering of the sanctuary.
Both accounts associate the dying king with his wrongs against Jerusalem and its temple; the other expresses this through vows to free the city and replace the plundered vessels.
Both connect Antiochus's miserable death in a foreign land with the evils he inflicted; this verse gives his own acknowledgment, while the other supplies the narrator's judgment.
Both associate Philip with the dying Antiochus, but his appointment over the kingdom here differs from the other account's description of transporting the body and fleeing to Egypt.
Both accounts describe arrangements for Antiochus's son to succeed him; this verse entrusts Philip with royal insignia and guidance, while the letter announces the son's appointment.
Both report Antiochus's death away from his homeland; the year supplied here is not inferred from the other account.
Both identify Antiochus Eupator as successor and connect Lysias with the kingdom's administration, though the accounts emphasize different aspects of his role.
The citadel's continuing threat to the holy places develops the earlier description of its lawless garrison as an ambush against the sanctuary.
The plan to remove the citadel's occupants extends Judas's earlier order to fight them while the sanctuary was being cleansed.
The alliance of citadel escapees and ungodly Israelites continues the hostility of the lawless garrison originally established against the sanctuary.
The petitioners profess continuing loyalty to the father's decrees, recalling Antiochus's policy of abolishing separate customs and the Israelites who accepted it.
The petition names the sanctuary and Beth-zur as fortified places, matching the two defensive projects undertaken after the dedication.
Both accounts depict Antiochus Eupator and Lysias mobilizing against Judea with support from hostile instigators; the dates and specific instigators in their accounts remain distinct.
The arrival of hired troops develops the earlier notice that Lysias recruited additional mercenaries after his defeat in Judea.
Both enumerate Eupator's infantry, cavalry, and war elephants, but the totals and stated year differ and are preserved as separate accounts.
Both accounts describe royal pressure on Beth-zur and vigorous Jewish resistance; the other also reports Judas sending provisions into the fortress.
In both accounts Judas moves to confront the royal invasion, but his encampment is Beth-zechariah here and near Modein there; these locations are not harmonized.
The Eleazar called Avaran who attacks the royal-looking elephant is the son of Mattathias introduced with that same byname.
Eleazar's willingness to give himself for his people and gain an everlasting name recalls Mattathias's call to give their lives for the covenant and receive an everlasting name.

Eleazar's giving himself to save his people exemplifies the willingness to surrender one's life for others commended in Jesus's saying about laying down one's life for friends; no prediction or identity is asserted.

Both invasion narratives include an elephant being stabbed, but here Eleazar dies beneath the fallen beast, while the other describes Judas's successful night raid; these are compared without treating them as one incident.
Beth-zur's shortage during the land's sabbath is situated within the law requiring the seventh year to be a rest from sowing, pruning, and ordinary harvest.

Both describe a negotiated settlement at Beth-zur; this account explains the surrender through lack of provisions in the sabbatical year, whereas the other emphasizes exchanged pledges and withdrawal.
The notice that it was the seventh year invokes the agricultural cycle in which the land is left to rest after six years of cultivation, helping explain the depleted stores.
Simon's arrival in Judea with evacuated Galilean families provides an earlier example of the refugees from surrounding nations whose consumption of provisions is reported here.
Judas's gathering of the Gileadite population for migration to Judah supplies another earlier influx behind the notice that refugees had consumed the remaining stores.
The renewed mention of Philip's commission explicitly recalls the dying king's appointment of him to guide his son into royal rule.
Both accounts make news about Philip's challenge at Antioch a reason for the royal side to seek accommodation with the Jews; their descriptions of his commission differ.
The pressure of affairs elsewhere helps explain the royal decision to negotiate in both accounts, though this verse also stresses dwindling manpower, food, and the strength of the besieged place.
The proposal of peace with the Jewish nation corresponds to the other account's settlement following the report about Philip; the terms and subsequent treatment of the sanctuary differ.
Restoration of the Jews' ancestral customs reverses Antiochus's earlier decrees forbidding their laws, sacrifices, Sabbaths, and circumcision, the very policy now acknowledged as the cause of revolt.
Both accounts report the royal side accepting a settlement with the Jews after internal political pressure, while presenting its circumstances and aftermath differently.
Both describe an oath accompanying the settlement; the following verse here records its violation, whereas the other narrative stresses honours shown to the temple.
This account says the king broke his oath and demolished the sanctuary wall; the companion account describes sacrifice, temple honours, and kind treatment, a difference left explicit.
Both conclude the expedition with the political problem involving Philip and a return toward Antioch; the battle to seize Antioch is stated here rather than supplied by the other account.

Both introduce Demetrius son of Seleucus arriving by sea and gaining the kingdom; this account mentions departure from Rome with a few men, while the other names Tripolis and a strong force and fleet.
The seizure of Antiochus and Lysias is part of the dynastic overthrow summarized in the other account as Demetrius doing away with Antiochus and his guardian.
Both accounts connect Demetrius's accession with the elimination of Antiochus and Lysias; this text specifies that the troops killed them.
Both portray Alcimus approaching Demetrius with an interest in the high priesthood; the other explicitly describes him as a former high priest seeking restoration.
Both accounts make Alcimus's party accuse Judas of destabilizing royal rule and harming the country, although their reported speeches use different charges.
The appeal for royal intervention corresponds to Alcimus's demand for action against Judas and the resulting punitive commission in the companion narrative; the envoys sent are described differently.
Bacchides, selected here as a trusted royal agent, is sent again after Nicanor's defeat, establishing the continuity of his role in Demetrius's interventions.
Both connect a royal military mission with imposing Alcimus as high priest; this commission is given to Bacchides, while the other passage gives it to Nicanor.
The new royal force's deceitful peaceful message repeats the earlier tribute collector's tactic of speaking peace before attacking Jerusalem.
The Hasideans seeking peace here are the named group previously described as strong supporters of the law who joined Mattathias's resistance.
The people's trust rests on Alcimus's Aaronic priesthood; in the other account Alcimus himself claims the high priesthood as his ancestral honour, without that claim guaranteeing his conduct.
The assurance of safety and sworn promise are directly contradicted by the killing of sixty men and the people's subsequent charge of oath-breaking.
The killing is related to a written word, and the quotation that follows draws on the psalm's slaughtered holy ones and blood around Jerusalem; the target uses the source's Greek Psalm 78 numbering.
The quotation combines the psalm's flesh of God's holy ones with blood poured around Jerusalem and the absence of anyone to bury them, retaining Greek Psalm 78 numbering.
The people's judgment that a sworn agreement has been broken recalls the preceding king's oath followed by his demolition of the sanctuary wall.
Bacchides's departure leaving Alcimus in charge is followed later by Demetrius sending both men into Judea again after Nicanor's destruction.
Alcimus's struggle for the high priesthood corresponds to the other account's explanation that he approached Demetrius to regain his former ancestral office.
Both accounts describe Alcimus returning to Demetrius with accusations that provoke action against Judas; the other places this complaint after Nicanor's friendly agreement with Judas.
Both accounts report Demetrius selecting Nicanor and ordering military action against Judas and his followers.
Both describe peace negotiations between Nicanor and Judas, but this account presents the overture as deceitful from the start, whereas the other describes a genuine period of goodwill.
Both describe an arranged personal meeting between Judas and Nicanor with concern about possible treachery; their presentation of Nicanor's original intentions differs.
This meeting conceals an attempt to seize Judas, whereas the other narrative describes a proper conference followed by Nicanor's attachment to him; the divergent portrayals remain explicit.
Both accounts describe Judas discerning danger in Nicanor's conduct and avoiding him, though the other places the intended betrayal after a royal order to break their settlement.
The priests' offering on behalf of the king has a precedent in the royal provision of sacrificial materials so that Jerusalem's priests could pray for the king and his sons.
Both accounts bring Nicanor to the temple while priests are offering sacrifices, followed by his demand for Judas; this account additionally describes their peaceful welcome and royal offering.
Nicanor's contemptuous, arrogant treatment of the priests corresponds to the other account's threat to destroy their sanctuary unless Judas is surrendered.
Both preserve Nicanor's sworn threat to destroy the temple unless Judas is delivered to him; the companion account adds demolition of the altar and a proposed temple for Dionysus.
Both describe the priests praying after Nicanor's threat, appealing to God to preserve the sanctuary He chose for His dwelling.
The priests appeal to the house chosen for God's name and His people's petitions, the functions emphasized in Solomon's prayer that God hear Israel praying toward this house.
Calling the temple a house of prayer echoes Isaiah's description of God's house of prayer; Isaiah extends the welcome to all nations, while this petition speaks of God's people.
Both prayers after Nicanor's threat ground their plea in God's gracious choice to have a temple among His people and seek its preservation.
The priests ask for judgment on Nicanor's insults, while Judas's later prayer in the companion account asks that the army coming in blasphemy be struck with terror.
Both accounts portray Judas praying before the decisive battle with Nicanor and appealing to the earlier deliverance from Sennacherib.
The angel's destruction of one hundred eighty-five thousand recalls the stated number and angelic action in the account of Sennacherib's defeated army.
Judas recalls the same angelic deliverance and casualty figure preserved in Isaiah's account of the Assyrian camp.
The remembered answer to royal blasphemy corresponds to the Assyrian reproach followed by prayer and an angel's destruction of the enemy commanders; Chronicles does not supply the number quoted here.
Both versions of Judas's prayer recall the angel killing one hundred eighty-five thousand, with the companion account explicitly naming Hezekiah and Sennacherib.
Both prayers ask for a present defeat of the enemy on the model of the former angelic deliverance and specifically identify the enemy's blasphemy.
Both accounts report Nicanor's defeat and death in the decisive battle; this account says he fell first, while the other describes recognition of his body after the fighting.
The thirteenth of Adar given as the battle date is the same date fixed for annual observance in the companion account.
Nicanor's troops flee when they see their commander dead, as the foreigners flee after David kills and beheads their champion; both flights lead to pursuit.
The enemy turning against itself under pursuit recalls Gideon's victory, in which the Lord turns each enemy sword against its neighbour; the surrounding battle descriptions differ.
Both accounts describe Nicanor's head and threatening hand being severed and displayed at Jerusalem as evidence of the defeat of his arrogant assault on the sanctuary.
The defeated enemy leader's head is brought to Jerusalem, as David brings the foreign champion's head there; the additional severed hand is distinctive to Nicanor's story.
The people's great rejoicing corresponds to the victorious army's joyful return, shouting, and blessing of God after Nicanor's fall.
Both accounts establish annual observance of the victory on the thirteenth of Adar; the companion account also identifies its relation to Mordecai's day.
The qualification that Judah's peace lasted only a few days anticipates Demetrius's renewed invasion after hearing of Nicanor's defeat.
The reputation of Roman friendship that attracts Judas leads to the relationship Jonathan later sends envoys to renew explicitly as an existing friendship and alliance.

The account of Rome demanding hostages from Antiochus the Great's dynasty supplies background to the earlier identification of Antiochus Epiphanes as a former hostage in Rome; it does not add an unstated hostage date.
Rome's reported fidelity to friends is illustrated later by its recognition of the Jews as friends and allies and its letters forbidding attacks on their country.
The reported absence of Roman diadems contrasts with Alexander's successors putting on diadems, a marked difference in the book's presentation of imperial power.
The Roman council chamber described here is the institution later entered by Jonathan's envoys to renew Jewish friendship and alliance.
Judas's original embassy to establish Roman friendship and alliance precedes Jonathan's embassy expressly sent to renew that relationship.
The later bronze tablets explicitly recall the friendship and alliance first established with Judas and then Jonathan, identifying this embassy's enduring diplomatic result.
The aim of removing the Greek yoke responds to the earlier royal policy suppressing Israel's laws, worship, and covenantal practices.
Both the original envoys and Jonathan's later delegation enter Rome's council chamber and present an alliance proposal on behalf of the Jewish leadership and nation.
The request to be enrolled as Roman allies and friends is reflected in the later Roman letter recognizing Jewish envoys as friends and allies renewing an existing agreement.
The alliance memorial inscribed on bronze tablets is matched by later bronze tablets renewing the friendship established with Judas and Jonathan.
The treaty's wish that sword and enemy remain far from the Jews takes practical form in the later Roman directive that rulers neither attack them nor support their enemies.
The clause covering war against Rome introduces a reciprocal defense obligation, balanced by the later clause covering war against the Jewish nation.
The Jews' obligation to fight wholeheartedly beside Rome is balanced by Rome's corresponding pledge to fight wholeheartedly beside the Jewish nation.

The treaty forbids supplying Rome's enemies; the later Roman letter likewise prohibits other rulers from allying with those making war against the Jews, extending the logic of withholding enemy support.
Rome's promise to support the Jews in war develops into a later circular directing kings and countries not to attack the Jews or assist their enemies.
The agreement established here is the former friendship and alliance that Jonathan later commissions named envoys to renew.
Rome's protest about Demetrius's heavy yoke responds to the king's earlier intervention against Judas and his supporters, including Bacchides's punitive mission.

The threat to intervene if the Jews suffer further harm anticipates the later Roman warning to rulers not to attack their Jewish allies; the later directive does not report this threatened war as having occurred.
